title: Santiago to the Mountain: The Golden Thread
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Santiago — La Casa de la Cordillera

stops.name: Santiago de Chile — Calle Santo Domingo, the birth
stops.campa: On the tenth of September, in a house on Calle Santo Domingo, Miguel Joaquín Diego del Carmen Serrano Fernández is born into an old Chilean family, criollo and Basque and Castilian, that came to the kingdom with the conquest. Beyond the flat roofs of the capital the Andes stand white and enormous, the eastern wall of the world. The child is set down at the foot of the cordillera that will be his temple and his cosmology to the end. He will call his life a single ascent toward the Mountain, and here, in the shadow of the snow, the ascent begins.
suggested_refs: Cordillera de los Andes above Santiago
sources: Memorias de Él y Yo, vol. I

stops.name: Valle del Claro — the seventeenth-century mansion
stops.campa: His mother Berta dies when he is five; three years on his father Diego follows her into the ground. Orphaned, Miguel and his brothers and sister pass into the keeping of the grandmother, Fresia Manterola de Serrano, between a Santiago townhouse and a seventeenth-century casona in the Valle del Claro. In the country house the boy walks vineyards and old galleries where the dead of the family seem to linger; the early loss opens in him the wound he will spend his life sealing — the search for what does not die, for the Beloved beyond death, for A-Mor.
suggested_refs: Casona colonial del Valle del Claro
sources: Memorias de Él y Yo, vol. I

stops.name: Internado Nacional Barros Arana, Santiago
stops.campa: From 1929 he boards at the Internado Nacional Barros Arana, a school of Prussian severity and cold dormitories. Here the boy who has lost his parents finds a second family in books and in a circle of young writers; here too, he will say, the Germanophile spark is struck that will never leave him. He reads voraciously — the Romantics, Nietzsche, the sagas of the North — and begins to dream of a heroic order beyond the grey Republic, of initiation, of a hidden brotherhood into which a man might be reborn.

stops.name: Santiago — the Generation of '38 and the poet Huidobro
stops.campa: In the cafés of Calle San Diego and Avenida Matta the youth of the Generation of '38 gather — Héctor Barreto, Teófilo Cid, the strange Juan Emar. Serrano moves among them as poet, kin to the great creacionista Vicente Huidobro, who is his uncle and whose praise he covets. At twenty-one he assembles an anthology of the Chilean realist tale, a milestone of the national letters. He is a poet first; a poet, the exiled Armando Uribe will call him at the last, 'the truest poet.' The avant-garde and the mountain-worship live in him together.

stops.name: Santiago — the Seguro Obrero massacre, Calle Morandé
stops.campa: On the fifth of September the young Chilean National Socialists rise, are cornered in the Caja del Seguro Obrero on Calle Morandé, surrender, and are shot down almost to a man. The massacre scars Serrano forever; the sacrificed youths become, in his memory, martyrs of a doomed heroism. He turns from the left toward which Barreto's death had pushed him, seeks out the movement's leaders, and thereafter reads politics as sacred war. The blood on Morandé is, for him, an initiation into loss and defeated nobility — a wound he will never let close.
suggested_refs: Seguro Obrero massacre memorial, Cementerio General

stops.name: Santiago — the review La Nueva Edad
stops.campa: From July of 1941 Serrano launches his own fortnightly, La Nueva Edad — 'The New Age' — a review of politics and letters through which he casts Chile's neutrality against the tide of the war. Here, in the printed word, he first sets down the mythic frame that will govern his whole cosmos: a New Age dawning, a hidden order of initiates, a war of the visible against the invisible. His uncle Huidobro praises his prose. The poet of the mountain has become the herald of a myth he will spend seven decades enlarging.

stops.name: The Andes above Santiago — the mountain as temple
stops.campa: In the great climbs of his youth Serrano goes up into the cordillera as into a cathedral. The Andes are for him no mere geology but the visible spine of the sacred, a temple of stone and light where the air thins and the self burns away. On the high glaciers he feels the presence he will chase across the world — the Mountain that is also the Self, the pole of the spirit. Mountaineering, for him, is prayer; the summit is a threshold. Every later journey, to the ice and to the Himalaya, is a repetition of this first ascent.

segments.name: La Antártica — The Ice and the Poles

stops.name: Valparaíso — embarkation for the Antarctic
stops.campa: Serrano ships out from the Chilean coast with the Second Chilean Antarctic Expedition, carried south as a reporter for Zig-Zag and El Mercurio, his despatches read the length of the Republic. He goes, he will confess only years later, with a secret aim: to draw near the polar entrances of the legend, the openings at the ends of the earth into the Inner World. The Southern Ocean opens grey and vast before the bow. He is sailing not merely toward Antarctica but toward the mystery that will hold his cosmology to the last day of his life.

stops.name: Base Soberanía, Greenwich Island, South Shetlands
stops.campa: The expedition raises Base Soberanía — Sovereignty — on the black shore of Greenwich Island, the second Chilean station in Antarctica. Serrano walks among the huts and the ice in a light that never wholly dies, keeping his despatches while his mind runs beneath the glacier. Here Chile plants her flag at the bottom of the world; here Serrano begins to read the white continent as a text of Atlantis and Hyperborea, a great white island fallen from the sky, and to ask whether the defeated of the war have withdrawn, as the legend says, into warm oases hidden under the eternal ice.

stops.name: Deception Island — the narrow entrance of the caldera
stops.campa: The ship threads the Neptune's Bellows, the narrow gap in the drowned volcano of Deception Island, into the black flooded caldera where the beaches steam and the ice draws back from waters warmed by the fire below. Here is the very image of his myth made land: a warm oasis ringed by ice, a hidden harbour entered by a single narrow mouth. On the voyage he is reading Jung on the ego and the unconscious, and the whole white continent turns to a country of archetypes. He will write of penetrating again, in the spirit, through the narrow entrance of Deception Island.

stops.name: The unnamed massif — the mountain that bore his name
stops.campa: In gratitude for his voyage the expedition names a mountain of the white land for him, so that for a season a peak at the bottom of the world carries the name Serrano — though later the name is taken away and given to another. It is, for the mythographer, a perfect emblem: a mountain of ice bearing his name and then unnamed, a summit at the pole, present and erased at once. He has planted himself, if only for a moment, upon the very axis of the earth that his cosmos will make its centre.

stops.name: The South Pole — the entrance to the Inner Earth (Symmes's hollow)
stops.campa: In Serrano's cosmos the pole is a door. Below the axis, where Symmes long ago set the mouth of his hollow world, lies the entrance to the Inner Earth — the warm oasis at the heart of the ice, the refuge of the Hyperboreans and of the Führer who, he insists, did not die but withdrew. The two openings of the planet answer each other, north and south; the poles are not places but thresholds. He gazes across the ice-cap toward that hidden mouth. His whole later mythology — Nos, the resurrection, the return — will hang upon this conviction born on the ice.

stops.name: La Antártica y otros mitos — the book of the ice
stops.campa: Back in Santiago he writes La Antártica y otros mitos — 'Antarctica and Other Myths' — the first of the books in which the white continent becomes scripture. He weaves the indigenous vision of a great white island in the sky, the drowned tale of Atlantis, the survival of the vanquished beneath the ice, into one myth of the pole. The Caleuche, the ghost-ship of Chiloé, sails in his pages like a submarine beneath the Antarctic sea. The reporter's despatches have become a cosmology; the ice has entered him and will not thaw.
stops.quote: The Caleuche sails like a submarine. Will she cross beneath the ice of the South Pole?
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, La Antártica y otros mitos (1948)
suggested_refs: La Antártica y otros mitos, first edition

stops.name: Monte Melimoyu, Patagonia — the antipode of Kailash
stops.campa: In the far south of Chile the twin volcanic horns of Melimoyu rise from the rainforest, and Serrano fixes upon this mountain as the muse and pole of his native land — the exact antipode, he declares, of tantric Kailash in the Himalaya, joined to it across the round of the earth by lines of force. Melimoyu is a portal, an energetic gate to the other realms. Between the two sacred summits, the one in Patagonia and the one in Tibet, he will string his golden thread, and he will carry the errand of that thread to the very court of India.

segments.name: El Ella — The Wound of A-Mor

stops.name: The meeting of Irene — the Beloved found
stops.campa: In October he meets Irene Klatt, a young German woman of grave beauty, her lungs already failing. In her he beholds Her — Ella — the Beloved his orphaned childhood had prophesied, the feminine pole of his own soul made flesh. For a season they are He and She, the archetypal union, the two halves of a single androgyne turning toward each other across the abyss. He believes he has found at last the immortal love the Grail promises, the love that is A-Mor, without-death.

stops.name: The death of Irene — the birth of the doctrine of A-Mor
stops.campa: In March She dies, and the wound of his childhood is torn open to the bone. He never recovers; he will say he never wishes to. Out of the loss he forges his central mystery: that Amor read backward is Roma, the way of the mortal world, but that Amor itself is a-mor, without-death — a love consummated not in the flesh but through initiation, so that the parted lovers are made immortal and eternal, reunited beyond the poles. The dead Beloved becomes his Beatrice, his guide up the mountain. El/Ella is born of this grave.
suggested_refs: ELELLA: Book of Magic Love, first edition

stops.name: New Delhi — credentials to Nehru
stops.campa: Following the old family tradition of service, Serrano enters the diplomatic corps and is sent to India, where he will remain the better part of a decade. Presenting himself to Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, he declares — half diplomat, half mystagogue — that he has come to bind together two mountains at the ends of the earth. The Republic's envoy and the seeker of the interior Kailash are one man. In New Delhi he befriends Nehru and his daughter Indira, Krishna Menon and the leading spirits of the young nation, and turns his eyes toward the Himalaya.
stops.quote: I have come to establish a relationship between Mount Kailash and Mount Melimoyu.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, reported words on presenting credentials to Nehru

stops.name: Benares — the burning ghats on the Ganges
stops.campa: He goes down to Benares, oldest of cities, where the dead are given to the fire on the ghats above the Ganges and the ash slides into the holy river. The Chilean who lost his parents and his Beloved to death stands before a whole civilisation that has made a sacrament of it. Pilgrims descend into the grey water at dawn; the pyres never go out. Here the doctrine of A-Mor and the resurrection finds its eastern mirror — death not as ending but as passage, the river bearing the soul on toward the far shore beyond the poles.

stops.name: The ashrams of the Himalayan foothills
stops.campa: Beyond the embassy's business Serrano ascends toward the sources of the Ganges, seeking out the yogis and the sannyasins in their ashrams below the snows. He sits at the feet of sages, learns the postures and the breath, tastes the disciplines of Yoga and Tantra. He is convinced that here, in the mountain solitudes of India, waits the secret order of his own Chilean master, the brotherhood that spans the poles. The East does not convert him; it confirms him. He reads its gods through his own myth, and finds Kailash, Melimoyu and the Antarctic pole to be one Mountain.

stops.name: Toward Kailash — the mountain found within
stops.campa: He longs to stand at Kailash itself, the tantric axis of the world, but the sacred mountain lies in Tibet now shut behind the Chinese occupation, and the road is closed. So he makes the pilgrimage inward. He declares that he has reached not the outer, material Kailash but its inner aspect — the mountain of the spirit, present within the seeker, needing no passport. The temple, he concludes, is not of the external world but of the plane within oneself. It is the same verdict he will one day pronounce upon the City of the Caesars: the true sanctuary is interior.

stops.name: The Himalaya of exile — welcoming the Dalai Lama
stops.campa: In the spring of 1959 the young Fourteenth Dalai Lama crosses the passes out of occupied Tibet into India, and Serrano — alone among Western envoys — goes up into the Himalaya to receive him in exile. A friendship forms between the Chilean seeker of the interior Kailash and the god-king driven from the roof of the world. His son José will later remember journeys to the Hindu Himalaya to meet the Dalai Lama after the escape, and the father's saying that an Avatar can never truly die. The exiled sage and the mountain-mystic meet on the high road.
suggested_refs: Photograph: Serrano and the Dalai Lama

stops.name: The Serpent of Paradise — the book of India
stops.campa: From the Indian years come his eastern books — The Visits of the Queen of Sheba, for which the aged Jung himself consents to write a preface, and The Serpent of Paradise, the record of his pilgrimages. In these pages the diplomat vanishes and the initiate speaks: the coiled serpent of the spine, the awakening fire, the Beloved sought through the disciplines of the body, the interior Kailash. India has given him a language for the myth the ice first whispered. The Queen of Sheba, Jung had warned him, is only for a magic kind of love, never for matrimony.
stops.quote: The Queen of Sheba is only for a magic kind of love, never for matrimony.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung to Serrano, in C.G. Jung and Hermann Hesse: A Record of Two Friendships
suggested_refs: The Serpent of Paradise, first edition
The Visits of the Queen of Sheba (Jung preface)

segments.name: El Círculo Hermético — Jung and Hesse

stops.name: Montagnola — first at the table of Hermann Hesse
stops.campa: Above Lake Lugano, in the Italian corner of Switzerland, the old poet of Siddhartha keeps his house at Montagnola. Serrano climbs to it in the summer of 1951 and is received. It is the first thread of the friendship of a lifetime. Hesse, who has walked the same eastward road, recognises the pilgrim from the ends of the earth; they will write to one another until the poet's death. In Hesse's rooms Serrano feels himself admitted at last into a company he has sought since boyhood — the Hermetic Circle, where only the right guests meet.

stops.name: Küsnacht — the house of Jung on Lake Zürich
stops.campa: Returning from Montagnola, Serrano resolves to see the old sage of Küsnacht again, and telephones the house by the lake at the sign of the Latin motto over the door. On the fifth of May Jung receives him in his study and speaks as from within a dream, of the Queen of Sheba, of the polygamy of the soul, of the perilous stages of the mystic wedding, of following Nature. The Chilean sits before the last of the great magi of the age. Here, on Lake Zürich, the corpus keeps its dearest correspondence: this stop faces the journey of Jung, and the letter that lives upon our own chain.
stops.quote: Somewhere there was once a Flower, a Stone, a Crystal, a Queen, a King, a Palace, a Lover and his Beloved... Such is Love, the Mystic Flower of the Soul. This is the centre, the Self.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung to Serrano, Küsnacht; in A Record of Two Friendships
suggested_refs: House of Jung, Küsnacht (VOCATVS ATQVE NON VOCATVS)

stops.name: Bollingen — the Tower and the carved stone
stops.campa: Jung takes the Chilean up the lake to Bollingen, to the round tower of stone he raised with his own hands, a dwelling without electric light where the old man lives as in the Middle Ages. In the garden stands the great cube Jung cut and carved himself, the Bollingen Stone, its faces graven with the little cloaked Telesphoros and Latin mottoes of the alchemists. For Serrano, the seeker of the sacred mountain and the interior stone, this hewn cube by the water is a revelation: the Self made mineral, the philosopher's stone set down at the lake's edge.

stops.name: Küsnacht — the last letter of Jung (14 September 1960)
stops.campa: From the house on the lake, near the end, Jung writes to the Chilean a letter that Serrano will guard as a testament — a document, he says, of great importance, in which the old man sets down his last thoughts on the nature of the world and of his own labour. In it Jung tells how the ancient Gods never died but sleep in us, how Wotan in reality retained his vitality and returned; how man is a top animal exiled on a speck of planet, cosmically isolated, not the master in his own house. And at the last he confides that he guards his light and his treasure — most precious not only to himself but to the darkness of the Creator, who needs Man to illuminate his Creation. The corpus keeps this letter upon its own chain.
stops.quote: I am guarding my light and my treasure, convinced that nobody would gain and I myself would be badly, even hopelessly injured, if I should lose it. It is most precious not only to me, but above all to the darkness of the Creator, who needs Man to illuminate his Creation.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung to Miguel Serrano, Küsnacht, 14 September 1960; in A Record of Two Friendships

stops.name: Montagnola — 'the Hermetic Circle', 22 January 1961
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of January, snowflakes drifting past the window, Serrano takes lunch with Hesse at Montagnola. When the Chilean marvels at his fortune in having met both the poet and the sage, Hesse answers that nothing happens by chance — that here only the right guests meet, that this is the Hermetic Circle. The words seal the whole meaning of Serrano's wandering: the friendships were no accident but a summons, a gathering of the initiated across the mountains and the ice. It is one of the last of their meetings; the poet has months to live.
stops.quote: Nothing ever happens by chance. Here, only the right guests meet. This is the Hermetic Circle.
stops.quote_source: Hermann Hesse to Serrano, Montagnola, 22 January 1961; in A Record of Two Friendships

stops.name: Küsnacht — the death of Jung, 6 June 1961
stops.campa: On the sixth of June the sage dies in his house at Küsnacht, and a great storm is said to break over the lake, lightning striking the poplar in his garden. Hesse follows him into the ground within two months. Serrano, bereft of both his fathers of the spirit, gathers the letters and the last conversations and begins the book that will carry their voices — C.G. Jung and Hermann Hesse: A Record of Two Friendships. Through him the two old men of the Swiss lakes speak on. He is now the sole surviving guest of the Hermetic Circle.
stops.quote: Nobody understands what I mean. Only a poet could begin to understand.
stops.quote_source: C. G. Jung to Serrano; in A Record of Two Friendships
suggested_refs: A Record of Two Friendships, first English edition

segments.name: El Danubio — The Balkan and Austrian Years

stops.name: Belgrade — ambassador to Yugoslavia
stops.campa: From India the Republic sends him to the Balkans, ambassador to Tito's Yugoslavia at Belgrade where the Danube takes the Sava. He moves through the marshal's court, arranging Tito's own visit to Chile, a servant of the state by day and a mythographer by night. In the old crossroads of empires, on the fault between the Latin and the Slav worlds, he reads the landscape as ever through his myth. The diplomat's postings are, to him, stations of a single pilgrimage; every capital is a stop on the road up the Mountain.
suggested_refs: Belgrade at the confluence of Sava and Danube

stops.name: Vienna — envoy on the Danube, credentials to Bulgaria
stops.campa: His last and longest embassy is Vienna, whence he serves also to Bulgaria — presenting his credentials at Sofia in December of 1965 — and represents Chile before the Atomic Energy Agency and the industrial-development body on the Danube. In the imperial city of Vienna, in the heart of the German-speaking world he has revered since Barros Arana, he seeks out the old surviving figures of the defeated cause, gathering them into his private mythology. Here, on the great river, the ambassador spends the last years before the recall that will end his diplomatic life.

stops.name: Sofia — credentials to Bulgaria, 10 December 1965
stops.campa: On the tenth of December he presents his credentials at Sofia as Chile's first extraordinary ambassador to Bulgaria, one more capital of the socialist East added to his circuit. He crosses the Iron Curtain as a matter of protocol, moving between Vienna and the Balkan courts. In these grey Cold-War capitals the mythographer keeps his double life intact: the correct envoy of a small Andean republic, and, beneath, the reader of ley-lines and hidden orders, forever mapping the visible embassies onto the invisible geography of his cosmos.

stops.name: Madrid — the surviving figures of the defeated cause
stops.campa: Out of Vienna the ambassador travels to the corners of Europe where the vanquished of the war have gone to ground — to Madrid and the Iberian exile, seeking out the old aviators and soldiers of the lost cause, Rudel and Skorzeny, Degrelle in his Spanish refuge, Hanna Reitsch. In them Serrano reads not defeated men but survivors of a cosmic reverse, keepers, in his mythology, of the same secret withdrawn beneath the poles. He gathers their stories into his private cosmos, threads of the golden cord. The historian sees fugitives; the mythographer sees Hyperboreans in exile.

stops.name: Montségur — the pog of the Cathars, Languedoc
stops.campa: In the Languedoc he climbs the pog of Montségur, the last citadel of the Cathars, where in 1244 more than two hundred Perfect Ones walked singing into the crusaders' fire rather than recant. For Serrano this scorched mountain is the western Kailash, a pole of the Grail. He tells how, among the ruined walls, great arms of stone opened and a transparent emanation came to him — a sublime, superhuman love that moved him to tears. The mountain of the heretics answers the mountains of the ice and the Himalaya. This stop faces Molay's Templars and the corpus's own heresies.
stops.quote: Large arms of stone opened and a transparent emanation came to me, of sublime, superhuman love, which moved me to tears.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, on Montségur; in El/Ella, Book of Magic Love
suggested_refs: Field of the Burned (Prat dels Cremats)

stops.name: Montségur — the Grail as the stone of Lucifer's crown
stops.campa: On the burnt summit Serrano completes his gnosis of the Grail. The stone the Cathars hid, he teaches, is no cup but a jewel fallen from the crown of Lucifer — Earendel, the morning star — struck loose in his combat in the heavens when Hyperborea and Atlantis were destroyed. The Cathars were the guardians of the green ray, the keepers of Solar Kristianity, and their pyre at Montségur is a station of the same defeat that runs through the Templars, the vanquished of the war, the interior Kailash. All his mountains are one mountain, and the Grail-stone waits within it.
stops.quote: The Grail, hidden by the Cathars, was a jewel fallen from the Crown of Lucifer, broken in his combat in the heavens, when Hyperborea and Atlantis were destroyed.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, NOS, Book of the Resurrection

segments.name: El Cordón Dorado — The Return and the Mythology

stops.name: Santiago — the recall from the diplomatic service
stops.campa: With the election of Salvador Allende the mythographer is stripped of his embassy and dismissed from the service of the state he has represented for seventeen years. The public career is over. Serrano reads the recall not as a defeat but as a release into his true vocation: from now on he will build in the open the cosmos he has carried since the ice. The diplomat becomes wholly the myth-maker. He withdraws from the Republic's business to the labour that will fill the remaining forty years — the writing of the Golden Thread.

stops.name: Montagnola — the exile in Hesse's own house
stops.campa: Dismissed, Serrano crosses again to Switzerland and settles above Lake Lugano in the Casa Camuzzi at Montagnola — the very house where Hermann Hesse had lived and written for twenty years. In the poet's rooms the pilgrim closes a circle: the man who first climbed to Hesse's door in 1951 now keeps that door himself, tenant of the Hermetic Circle's own address. Here, in the years of exile, he broods over the great books to come, the Grail and the poles and the resurrection gathering toward the Cordón Dorado.

stops.name: El/Ella, Book of Magic Love
stops.campa: From the exile at Montagnola comes El/Ella: Libro del Amor Mágico — 'He/She: Book of Magic Love' — the book of the doctrine born at Irene's grave. In it He and She are the two poles of the one divine being, sundered and seeking reunion through the tantric way, through A-Mor without-death. The dead Beloved is raised into the eternal feminine, the guide up the mountain. Of all his books it is the one his readers hold nearest the heart of the myth — the love-mysticism that underlies even the war-cosmology, the tears that opened at Montségur set down as scripture.
suggested_refs: ELELLA: Book of Magic Love, first edition

stops.name: Santiago — El Cordón Dorado, the Golden Thread
stops.campa: He publishes El Cordón Dorado — the Golden Thread — the first panel of the great mythological cycle he now unfolds, in which he narrates a hidden cosmos of Hyperborea and the Black Sun, of the vanquished withdrawn beyond the poles, of an initiatory order stretching from Atlantis to the Andes. It is the myth he has authored across a lifetime, the strung thread that joins Melimoyu to Kailash to the Antarctic door to the burnt pog of the Cathars. Whatever the world makes of its dark matter, it is his own cosmos, built stone by stone from the ice up.

stops.name: Santiago — the return to Chile at Santa Lucía
stops.campa: In 1980 the wanderer comes home, to an apartment in the Barrio Bellas Artes beneath the green hill of Santa Lucía in the heart of Santiago, again at the foot of the cordillera where his life began. From here he writes NOS: Book of the Resurrection, the book of the return of the vanquished and of the dead Beloved, of the polar door reopening. The old poet keeps a kind of court; disciples climb to his rooms. His life has bent back upon its origin: the orphan of the Andes, grown old, dwells once more in the shadow of the sacred mountain.
suggested_refs: NOS: Book of the Resurrection, first edition

stops.name: Santiago — Adolf Hitler, el Último Avatãra
stops.campa: He publishes the central panel of his war-cycle, Adolf Hitler, el Último Avatãra — in his mythology the tenth and last avatar of the Hindu reckoning, the incarnation that closes an age, a figure of Wotan risen at the end of the Kali Yuga. It is the darkest chamber of the cosmos he has authored, the myth by which he reads the whole catastrophe of the century as sacred defeat and coming return. Set down here as the mythos he made, not as any truth of the world, it is the pole of his esoteric Hitlerism: the vanquished as the awaited, withdrawn beyond the ice, to come again.
suggested_refs: Adolf Hitler, el Último Avatãra, first edition

stops.name: Santiago — Memorias de Él y Yo, the alchemy of a life
stops.campa: In his old age Serrano sets down his life in four great volumes, the Memorias de Él y Yo — 'Memoirs of He and I' — reckoned among the finest autobiographies in the Chilean tongue. He orders the story by the colours of alchemy: the black of the nigredo, the white of the albedo, the red of the rubedo, the gold of the return. The orphaning, the mountains, the ice, the Beloved, Jung and Hesse, Kailash and Montségur — all are gathered as stations of a single Work, a life read as the transmutation of lead into the gold of the interior Mountain.
suggested_refs: Memorias de Él y Yo, four volumes

stops.name: Santiago — death at the foot of the cordillera
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of February, in his apartment beneath Santa Lucía, a stroke takes Miguel Serrano at ninety-one, at the foot of the same Andes over which he was born. He dies as he lived, certain that an Avatar can never truly die, that the parted lovers are reunited beyond the poles, that the golden thread runs on unbroken. The poet of the mountain lays down the pen after nine decades of building his myth. Outside the window the cordillera stands white and enormous, the eastern wall of the world, unchanged since it first looked down on the newborn on Calle Santo Domingo.
stops.quote_source: Miguel Serrano, recalled by his son José Serrano Rosselot

stops.name: Cementerio General de Santiago — the last road, past the martyrs
stops.campa: He is carried into the Cementerio General, more than a hundred following — kin, writers, disciples of the myth. The cortège takes a deliberate road, and the coffin halts before the memorial of the Seguro Obrero, the fallen youths of 1938 whose massacre had turned him seventy years before. The circle closes at the graveside where it opened: the martyrs of his young manhood receive the old mythographer at the end. He is laid down in the earth of Santiago, beneath the cordillera, the golden thread — in his own faith — passing on beyond the poles.
